modules.title: Ruby Language Core
modules.intro: Ruby interview questions for experienced backend engineers start with the language object model — everything in Ruby is an object, including nil, true, and integers. This module covers the questions interviewers actually ask: the difference between == and equal? and eql? and <=>, how Symbol interning works and when to use Symbol vs String, freeze vs frozen? vs dup, the truthiness rules (only nil and false are falsy), mutable vs immutable types, the frozen_string_literal pragma, and the small comparisons that recur in every round. Each answer is structured for a 45-minute interview: the direct answer, the why, an idiomatic Ruby example, and the trade-off. No Java-flavored code — every snippet uses last-expression return, idiomatic naming, and proper Ruby conventions.

modules.title: Ruby OOP Advanced
modules.intro: Ruby OOP interview questions probe deeper than class and object basics. This module covers the questions mid-to-senior interviews actually ask: the full BasicObject → Object → Module → Class hierarchy, MRO method lookup order, open classes and monkey-patching (with risks), duck typing and respond_to? vs is_a?, self in different contexts, class variables (@@) vs class-level instance variables, attr_accessor internals, the Comparable mixin contract, and the difference between inheritance and composition in Ruby. Every answer includes an idiomatic Ruby code shape and surfaces the trade-off the interviewer is really listening for — when open classes become a maintenance problem, when duck typing breaks down, when inheritance is the wrong tool.

modules.title: Blocks, Procs & Lambdas
modules.intro: Blocks, Procs, and Lambdas are the most-tested Ruby language topic in intermediate and senior interviews. This module covers every angle interviewers probe: block syntax (do/end vs curly braces and their precedence), yield and block_given?, explicit &block capture, converting a method to a proc with &method(:name), Proc.new vs proc vs lambda vs stabby lambda, the four key differences between Proc and Lambda (return behavior, arity enforcement, === and lambda?), closures and captured variables, Proc#curry for partial application, symbol-to-proc shorthand &:method, and functional composition with << and >>. Every answer includes the code shape that makes the difference visible and explains when each form is the right tool.

modules.title: Modules & Mixins
modules.intro: Ruby modules and mixins replace multiple inheritance and are one of the most-probed intermediate interview topics. This module covers include vs extend vs prepend and how each one alters the MRO ancestors chain, the included/extended/prepended hooks, how Enumerable gives you map/select/sort/min/max/group_by for free if you implement each, how Comparable gives you all comparison operators for free if you implement <=>, module_function for utility modules, ActiveSupport::Concern and why it cleans up the included do block pattern, and the module as namespace pattern. Every answer traces the method lookup path so the interviewer can see you understand the ancestor chain, not just the syntax.

modules.title: Metaprogramming
modules.intro: Ruby metaprogramming interview questions separate candidates who know the syntax from those who understand the risks. This module covers method_missing and why respond_to_missing? must always accompany it, define_method for dynamic method generation, send vs public_send (and the security difference), class_eval and instance_eval, const_get and const_set, instance_variable_get and instance_variable_set, the inherited/included/extended/method_added lifecycle hooks, and DSL patterns (the class macro pattern that Rails associations use). Every answer includes a realistic use case, the debuggability trade-off, and the production warning: metaprogramming makes stack traces harder to read and performance harder to profile.

modules.title: Ruby Concurrency
modules.intro: Ruby concurrency questions are a litmus test for production experience. This module covers the MRI GVL (Global VM Lock) — what it prevents (true CPU parallelism for threads) and what it allows (IO-bound concurrency), Thread lifecycle and Thread.new, Mutex and synchronize for shared state, Queue and SizedQueue, Fiber as cooperative concurrency (not preemptive), Fiber vs Thread trade-offs, Ractor (Ruby 3) share-nothing model and message passing, the async gem event loop over Fibers, and Puma vs Unicorn concurrency models. Every answer names the failure mode — thread-safety bugs in shared mutable state, blocking the GVL in CPU-bound work, the cooperative-scheduling trap in Fiber.

modules.title: Rails MVC Core
modules.intro: Rails framework interview questions for experienced engineers go beyond the scaffold. This module covers the full Rails request lifecycle (router → middleware stack → controller → model → view/serializer → response), the Rack protocol and how any Ruby object with a call method becomes middleware, how the middleware stack is ordered and how to add custom middleware, the Zeitwerk autoloader and how constant lookup works, Rails engine vs mountable engine, config/initializers execution order, ActiveSupport::Notifications for instrumentation, and common scenario-based questions (why is my middleware not running, what happens when Zeitwerk can't find a constant, how do I debug the request lifecycle). Every answer traces the full path.

modules.title: Action Controller
modules.intro: Action Controller interview questions cover the layer Rails engineers spend most of their time in. This module covers before_action/after_action/around_action execution order and skip_before_action, strong parameters (params.require.permit) and why they exist as the Rails 4+ replacement for attr_accessible, sessions (cookie-based default vs server-side) and the security implications of each, cookies with Secure/HttpOnly/SameSite flags, flash messages and flash.now, respond_to format blocks for JSON vs HTML, render vs redirect_to and when each is correct, rescue_from for centralized error handling, ActionController::Live for SSE streaming, and concerns for shared controller logic. Each answer names the Rails convention and the escape hatch.

modules.title: Rails Routing
modules.intro: Rails routing interview questions test whether you understand how requests become controller actions. This module covers the 7 RESTful routes that resources generates and what HTTP method/path each maps to, nested routes and the recommended nesting depth limit (2 levels), member vs collection routes, namespace vs scope vs module for URL and controller organisation, route constraints (regex and custom constraint objects), named routes and the path/url helper distinction, mount for Rack apps and Rails engines, the root route, redirect shortcuts in routes.rb, and inspecting routes with rails routes and the --grep flag. Every answer includes the routes.rb snippet and the resulting URL pattern.

modules.title: Action View & Helpers
modules.intro: Rails view interview questions cover the rendering layer that most engineers underestimate. This module covers ERB syntax and the difference between <%= %> and <% %>, layouts and yield/content_for for composing pages, partials with locals and when to extract a partial, the difference between helpers (module methods), decorators (object wrappers), and ViewComponent (class-based components), form_with and how the CSRF token is injected automatically, link_to/button_to/image_tag helpers, html_safe and the XSS risk of raw, the Rails asset pipeline vs importmap vs jsbundling-rails decision, and rendering JSON from controllers without views. Every answer surfaces the security or performance implication.

modules.title: Active Support & Railtie
modules.intro: Active Support powers the Rails magic that engineers often take for granted. This module covers the ActiveSupport::Concern pattern and how it eliminates the included do base.extend ClassMethods boilerplate, time zones with Time.current vs Time.now (always use Time.current in Rails), config.time_zone and the TZInfo dependency, the commonly-used Active Support utilities (blank?/present?/presence, deep_merge, to_query, humanize/titleize/camelize/parameterize), ActiveSupport::Notifications for subscribing to Rails instrumentation events, the delegate macro for method forwarding, class_attribute vs cattr_accessor, memoization with ||= and the thread-safety caveat, and Railtie as the entry point for gems to hook into Rails initialization.

modules.title: Hotwire, Turbo & Stimulus
modules.intro: Hotwire and Turbo are the Rails 7/8 default frontend stack and increasingly common in Rails interviews. This module covers Turbo Drive (replaces full page navigation with AJAX morphing), Turbo Frames for partial page replacement without JavaScript, Turbo Streams for server-pushed real-time updates over WebSocket or SSE, the turbo_stream_from helper and how broadcasting works, Stimulus controller lifecycle (connect, disconnect, targets, values, actions), the importmap + Turbo + Stimulus default Rails 7 frontend stack, and the Hotwire vs React/Vue/Next.js decision (when Hotwire is enough and when a SPA is warranted). Every answer includes the trade-off that interviewers listen for: complexity, developer experience, and SEO.

modules.title: Active Record Core
modules.intro: Active Record interview questions are the most-asked Rails technical topic. This module covers the Active Record vs Data Mapper pattern distinction, the full CRUD API and bang vs non-bang method semantics, validation types (presence, uniqueness, format, numericality, custom validator objects), validation contexts, dirty tracking (changed?, previous_changes, will_save_change_to?), the complete callback execution order, the critical after_commit vs after_save difference (transaction boundary), default_scope and why it causes bugs, named scopes vs class methods, optimistic locking with :lock_version, pessimistic locking with with_lock, counter_cache, touch, and single table inheritance. Every answer shows the Rails code and surfaces the production trade-off.

modules.title: Active Record Associations
modules.intro: Rails associations are tested in almost every intermediate interview. This module covers belongs_to (required: true by default since Rails 5), has_one, has_many, has_many :through vs has_and_belongs_to_many (always prefer :through for extensibility), polymorphic associations with as: and source_type:, self-referential associations, the dependent: :destroy vs :nullify vs :restrict_with_error options and when each is correct, inverse_of and why it prevents duplicate object creation and validation errors, counter_cache, touch for cache invalidation, association callbacks (before_add/after_add/before_remove/after_remove), strict_loading for N+1 detection in development, and foreign_key/primary_key overrides. Every answer names the SQL generated.

modules.title: Active Record Query Interface
modules.intro: Active Record query performance is the most common Rails production problem and the most-tested topic in senior interviews. This module covers the N+1 query problem (diagnosis with Bullet gem, strict_loading!, and SQL log analysis), the three solutions (includes — auto-chooses strategy, preload — always a separate IN query, eager_load — always a LEFT OUTER JOIN needed when WHERE references the association), Arel for programmatic query building, find vs find_by vs where.first performance difference, find_each and find_in_batches for batch processing, pluck vs select (pluck skips AR object instantiation), exists? vs any? vs count, update_all vs looping, and EXPLAIN ANALYZE via to_sql. Every answer shows the SQL generated and the decision tree.

modules.title: Active Record Migrations
modules.intro: Rails migration interview questions test whether you can run schema changes safely in production. This module covers the change method and its reversible helpers (add_column/remove_column/add_index/rename_column), when to use up/down vs reversible do, zero-downtime migration patterns (add column without NOT NULL first, backfill asynchronously, add constraint after data is populated, remove column after code is deployed), the strong_migrations gem for detecting dangerous migrations, schema.rb vs structure.sql (always use structure.sql if you use database-specific features like partial indexes, triggers, or functions), index types (B-tree, partial, expression, GIN/GiST for PostgreSQL), foreign key constraints, and migration rollback strategy in CI/CD.

modules.title: Sequel & Raw SQL
modules.intro: Sequel and raw SQL questions come up when interviewers want to test whether you understand the ORM vs the database layer. This module covers the Sequel gem — Model vs Dataset API, explicit vs Active Record's implicit approach, Sequel plugins (timestamps, validation_helpers, associations), when raw SQL is the right tool (complex CTEs, window functions, COPY for bulk import, database-specific features), find_by_sql and connection.execute in Active Record, sanitize_sql_array for safe interpolation, the danger of string interpolation in SQL (SQL injection), and the Active Record vs Sequel trade-off (Sequel: more explicit, composable, multi-database; Active Record: Rails integration, convention, ecosystem).

modules.title: Rails API Mode
modules.intro: Rails API mode interview questions test whether you can build production-grade JSON APIs. This module covers ActionController::API vs ActionController::Base and what gets stripped, enabling CORS with rack-cors, the four serialization options and their trade-offs (Jbuilder: view templates, fast to write, slow to render at scale; Active Model Serializers: declarative, legacy; jsonapi-serializer: fastest, JSONAPI spec; Alba: fastest gem, modern), API versioning strategies (URL segment /api/v1, Accept header, query param — trade-offs for each), pagination with Kaminari vs Pagy vs cursor-based, rate limiting with Rack::Attack + Redis, OpenAPI documentation with Rswag, and RFC 7807 Problem+JSON for error responses.

modules.title: GraphQL Ruby
modules.intro: GraphQL Ruby interview questions test whether you understand not just the syntax but the production challenges. This module covers the graphql-ruby gem's object types, query type, and mutation type structure, resolver methods and how context flows through, the N+1 problem specific to GraphQL resolvers (every field resolver triggers its own query), solving N+1 with graphql-batch and the dataloader pattern, argument validation and custom scalars, Relay-spec connections for pagination, subscriptions over ActionCable (and why WebSocket scaling is different from HTTP), authentication via context[:current_user], introspection security (disabling in production), persisted queries, and the REST vs GraphQL decision framework.

modules.title: Authentication & Authorization
modules.intro: Authentication and authorization interview questions cover the most security-sensitive part of any Rails application. This module covers Devise (model concerns, Warden hooks, OmniAuth integration, devise-jwt for token auth), JWT structure (header.payload.signature), JWT validation and the algorithm confusion attack (always specify algorithm explicitly — never trust the alg header), Doorkeeper for OAuth 2.0 authorization server, OAuth 2.0 flows (authorization code vs client credentials vs implicit), refresh tokens and rotation, Pundit policy objects and policy_scope for row-level access control, CanCanCan Ability class and can?/cannot?, role-based vs attribute-based access control, API key authentication with database-stored hashed keys, and session vs token trade-offs for Rails APIs.

modules.title: Sidekiq Deep Dive
modules.intro: Sidekiq interview questions are mandatory in any Rails interview that involves background processing. This module covers Sidekiq architecture (Redis as the job store, Sidekiq server polling the list, worker thread pool), worker definition with include Sidekiq::Worker and sidekiq_options, perform_async vs perform_in vs perform_at, queue naming and priority, the retry mechanism with exponential backoff (the retry formula), the dead set for jobs that exhaust retries, job idempotency (mandatory — retries are guaranteed, not exceptional), the sidekiq-unique-jobs gem for deduplication, client-side and server-side middleware chains, Sidekiq::Web UI, sidekiq-cron for scheduled jobs, and Sidekiq vs Resque vs GoodJob vs Delayed::Job trade-offs. The failure-mode question is the depth marker: what happens to the job when the worker process is killed mid-perform?

modules.title: Active Job & Action Mailer
modules.intro: Active Job and Action Mailer interview questions test the glue layer between Rails business logic and async delivery. This module covers ApplicationJob and the perform method, perform_later vs perform_now, queue adapters and how to swap (Sidekiq, GoodJob, Resque, :inline for test, :test for assertions), job callbacks (before_perform, after_perform, around_perform), ActionMailer::Base vs ActionMailer::Parameterized mailers, delivery methods (smtp, sendgrid, ses via action-mailer-ses, letter_opener for dev), deliver_later vs deliver_now and the transaction safety argument for deliver_later, mail previews in development, testing mailers (have_enqueued_mail matcher, ActionMailer::Base.deliveries), and ActionMailbox for inbound email routing.

modules.title: Action Cable & Pub/Sub
modules.intro: Action Cable interview questions come up whenever Rails real-time features or WebSocket experience is required. This module covers Action Cable channel lifecycle (subscribed, unsubscribed, receive), how Action Cable hijacks the HTTP connection and upgrades to WebSocket, the Redis adapter for multi-process pub/sub (mandatory for multi-Puma-process or Kubernetes deployments), broadcasting with ActionCable.server.broadcast and the turbo_stream_from tag for Turbo integration, stream naming conventions and channel authentication/authorization, Turbo::StreamsChannel for Hotwire Turbo Streams, the SSE vs WebSocket vs long-polling trade-off (SSE for server-to-client only; WebSocket for bidirectional; long-polling for maximum compatibility), and scaling Action Cable (sticky sessions with load balancer, Redis pub/sub for multi-node).

modules.title: Design Patterns in Ruby
modules.intro: Design pattern interview questions in Ruby test whether you apply patterns idiomatically rather than porting Java solutions. This module covers SOLID in Ruby (SRP via service objects, OCP via modules and Protocols, LSP via duck typing contracts, ISP via small focused modules, DIP via constructor injection and repository pattern), service objects (when to extract, naming conventions — verb + noun: CreateOrder, ChargePayment, the call method pattern), form objects for multi-model forms, query objects for complex AR queries, value objects (Money, EmailAddress as Struct or Data class), decorator pattern with SimpleDelegator vs Draper gem, presenter/view model pattern, the interactor pattern (dry-transaction, Interactor gem), strategy via Proc/lambda, and observer via ActiveSupport::Notifications.

modules.title: Clean Architecture in Ruby
modules.intro: Clean and hexagonal architecture interview questions test senior-level design thinking in Ruby. This module covers hexagonal architecture in Rails (domain layer → ports → adapters, how to keep domain logic independent of Rails), the dry-rb ecosystem (dry-validation for input validation, dry-types for type-safe value objects, dry-monads for railway-oriented programming, dry-transaction for multi-step workflows), DDD aggregates and value objects in Ruby (rich domain model vs anemic AR model), domain events for cross-aggregate communication, Trailblazer and Hanami as framework-agnostic alternatives to Rails MVC, and the pragmatic question of when to introduce architecture layers (rule: wait for real pain, then extract).

modules.title: System Design Fundamentals
modules.intro: System design interview questions for Rails engineers require concrete numbers and Rails-specific implementation knowledge. This module covers caching strategies in Rails (fragment caching, Russian doll caching, HTTP caching with ETags and Last-Modified, Redis cache store), horizontal scaling of Puma and how thread count affects memory, read replicas with ActiveRecord::Base.connected_to, database sharding in Rails 6+ multi-database support, background job scaling on queue depth with Sidekiq, CDN and asset delivery, rate limiting patterns with Rack::Attack and Redis, feature flags with Flipper gem, and multi-tenancy approaches (row-level isolation with default_scope or concerns, schema-per-tenant with Apartment gem, database-per-tenant for maximum isolation). Every answer includes concrete capacity estimates.

modules.title: System Design Case Studies
modules.intro: System design case study questions with Rails context require phased walkthroughs with concrete capacity numbers. This module covers five canonical cases: URL shortener (10M URLs/day — Rails + PostgreSQL + Redis for hot lookups + Base62 encoding), news feed (fan-out-on-write vs fan-out-on-read at 100M DAU — Sidekiq for fan-out, Redis sorted sets for timeline), real-time chat (ActionCable + Redis pub/sub + PostgreSQL for persistence), notification service (Sidekiq batches + multi-channel delivery — APNs, FCM, email, SMS — with dead letter queue), and file upload pipeline (ActiveStorage + S3 direct upload + background variant generation). Every case includes FR/NFR identification, capacity estimation, component diagram, and the trade-off that broke the design tie.

modules.title: Rails Security
modules.intro: Rails security interview questions test whether you know what Rails protects you from by default and — critically — how engineers accidentally disable those protections. This module covers Rails' built-in CSRF protection (protect_from_forgery with: :exception and how the token works), XSS prevention via automatic HTML escaping in ERB (and the html_safe/raw danger), SQL injection prevention via parameterized queries (and the danger of string interpolation in where), mass assignment protection via strong parameters, clickjacking protection via X-Frame-Options, OWASP Top 10 mapped to Rails with concrete examples, the Content-Security-Policy header, SameSite cookie policy, session fixation and reset_session, SSRF via open-uri, and the security implications of config.force_ssl and HSTS.

modules.title: Auth, Secrets & Scanning
modules.intro: Authentication security, secrets management, and static analysis are tested in security-conscious Rails interviews. This module covers secrets management (Rails.application.credentials and the master.key workflow, environment variables in production, AWS Secrets Manager for rotation), bundler-audit for CVE scanning of gem dependencies (how to integrate in CI and what to do on a hit), Brakeman for Rails-specific SAST (what it detects — mass assignment, SQLi, XSS, redirect, command injection — and false positive triage), JWT security deep-dive (algorithm confusion attack where alg:none or HS256/RS256 swap allows forging tokens, always specify algorithm explicitly), bcrypt via has_secure_password and work factor, timing-safe comparison with ActiveSupport::SecurityUtils.secure_compare, and Dependabot for automated dependency updates.

modules.title: RSpec Advanced
modules.intro: RSpec interview questions for experienced Rails engineers go beyond describe and it blocks. This module covers the execution model (let is lazy — evaluated on first call, let! is eager — evaluated before each example), subject and described_class, shared examples (shared_examples_for + it_behaves_like) for DRY contract testing across multiple implementations, shared contexts (shared_context + include_context) for setup reuse, custom matchers with RSpec::Matchers.define for expressive test assertions, aggregate_failures for multiple expect without early exit, around hooks, metadata-based tagging and filtering, spec/rails_helper.rb vs spec_helper.rb (Rails vs pure Ruby setup), ActiveJob::TestHelper for job assertions, ActionMailer::TestHelper for mailer assertions, and testing concerns with a dummy host class.

modules.title: FactoryBot & Capybara
modules.intro: FactoryBot and Capybara are the standard Rails test data and system testing tools — and both have depth that separates senior candidates from juniors. This module covers FactoryBot factory definition, traits, sequences, associations, and the build_stubbed vs build vs create cost hierarchy (build_stubbed: no database hit, fastest; build: in-memory AR object; create: database write), after(:create) hooks and their performance cost, FactoryBot linting to catch invalid factories, Capybara visit/fill_in/click_button/have_text for system tests, js: true and headless Chrome configuration, have_current_path matcher, Shoulda Matchers for model validation testing, DatabaseCleaner strategies (transaction for unit tests, truncation for JS system tests that use multiple threads), and driven_by configuration.

modules.title: Test Doubles & Contract Testing
modules.intro: Test doubles, mocking, and contract testing are tested in every senior Rails interview that covers testing strategy. This module covers RSpec doubles (double vs instance_double vs class_double — verifying doubles catch interface drift), allow vs expect (stub vs mock distinction), stub_const for constant replacement, WebMock stub_request for HTTP call stubs (and why you must test the request shape, not just stub it away), VCR cassettes for recording/replaying external API calls (and the cassette staleness problem), the spy pattern for after-the-fact assertions, as_null_object for lenient doubles, the test isolation vs integration pyramid decision, Pact contract testing for Rails microservices (consumer-driven contracts), and the Ruby-specific depth marker: never mock what you don't own.

modules.title: Docker, Kamal & Deployment
modules.intro: Rails deployment interview questions test whether you can ship code to production safely. This module covers Rails-specific Dockerfile patterns (copy Gemfile and Gemfile.lock before source code for Docker layer caching, bundle install with --without development test, asset precompilation in the build stage so the production image doesn't need Node, non-root user for security, RAILS_ENV=production, multi-stage build to eliminate build tools from the final image), Kamal deploy.yml configuration, traefik as reverse proxy, rolling deploy strategy, Heroku Procfile (web: bundle exec puma, worker: bundle exec sidekiq), GitHub Actions for Rails CI (ruby/setup-ruby with bundler-cache, rspec, rubocop, docker build and push), zero-downtime deploy patterns, and the DATABASE_URL environment variable pattern.

modules.title: Observability & Production
modules.intro: Production observability interview questions separate engineers who have shipped from those who have only developed locally. This module covers structured logging with Lograge (single-line JSON replacing Rails' multi-line format) and Semantic Logger, correlation IDs propagated via Rack middleware or Thread.current, rack-mini-profiler for SQL and rendering time in development, Skylight vs Scout APM vs Datadog APM for production traces, derailed_benchmarks and memory_profiler for memory profiling, stackprof for CPU profiling, rbspy for production profiling without restart, Sentry error tracking (capture_exception, release tracking, traces_sample_rate), N+1 detection in production via strict_loading and SQL log analysis, the four golden signals (p99 latency, req/s, error rate, saturation), SLI/SLO/SLA for Rails apps, and the blameless post-mortem format.

modules.title: Behavioral
modules.intro: Behavioral interview questions for Ruby engineers require first-person stories grounded in real Rails work. This module covers the STAR method (Situation, Task, Action, Result) applied to Rails projects, self-introduction for an experienced Ruby developer, conflict resolution stories (the Rails monolith vs microservices debate is the most common), failure stories with reflection (the N+1 you introduced in production, the Rails upgrade that broke something unexpected, the Sidekiq job you wrote before you understood idempotency), the weakness question framed as active growth, delivering under pressure (production incident response, upgrade deadline), and the reflection beat that separates a rehearsed answer from a self-aware one. Stories should feel like they happened at a real Rails shop, with named tools and specific consequences.

modules.title: Engineering Practices
modules.intro: Engineering practices interview questions test whether you think like an engineer who will make the team better, not just a coder who ships features. This module covers code review culture (anchor on intent and correctness first, style last — use RuboCop for style so humans focus on design), Architecture Decision Records (ADR template: context, decision, consequences — how to write one for a service object refactor or a Rails upgrade), technical debt strategy in a Rails app (identifying high-interest debt, the strangler fig pattern for Rails monolith decomposition, when to pay debt vs when to ship), mentoring stories (how you helped a junior understand Active Record callbacks or refactor a god model), and technical leadership signals (how you drive technical decisions without authority, how you run a post-mortem, how you propose a Rails upgrade).
